caption: Part of the southern tidal tail of the Antennae Galaxies, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Young blue stars crowd this view, strung along a stream of gas, while many red background galaxies peek through from far beyond. Zoom in and the field is also filled with thousands of faint red stars. This is a stretch of the southern tail thrown out by the Antennae Galaxies, NGC 4038 and NGC 4039, a pair of galaxies in the middle of merging.

The blue stars formed only recently, out of gas that has piled up along the backbone of the tail. The two galaxies began interacting a few hundred million years ago, and scientists treat them as the textbook example of a galaxy merger, a benchmark for testing ideas about how galaxies change over time.

The faint red stars matter for another reason. Red giant stars cannot shine brighter than a certain limit, so their measured brightness works as a distance marker. Using them, astronomers concluded the Antennae sit closer than once believed.
explore: The new measurement put the pair about 45 million light-years away, compared with the earlier best estimate of 65 million light-years. The Antennae rank among the nearest merging galaxies known, which is part of why they are studied so closely.

understand.summary: This view comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters in visible light and the near-infrared. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The near-infrared part of the data is invisible to the eye, and the thousands of faint red stars are far too dim to see without a large telescope.

alt: A dark field scattered with young blue stars along a band of gas, with many small red background galaxies and faint red stars.

caption: The halo of the giant elliptical galaxy Messier 87, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt Telescope
story: A huge, faint halo of light surrounds the giant elliptical galaxy Messier 87 in this very deep image, with many other galaxies scattered around it. These neighbours belong to the Virgo Cluster, and Messier 87 is the biggest of them all.

Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded collections of mostly older stars, and they are thought to grow partly by swallowing smaller galaxies. This picture holds evidence of just that. In the upper right part of the halo there is an excess of light, and it lines up with a clue from inside the galaxy: the way its planetary nebulae are moving.

Together, these are the final surviving traces of a medium-sized galaxy that collided with Messier 87 not long ago, in cosmic terms. Apart from this faint excess of light and the telltale motions of the planetary nebulae, little else in the picture records that the smaller galaxy was ever there.
explore: At the top right of the frame sit two galaxies that astronomers have nicknamed "the Eyes". Like the many other galaxies scattered around Messier 87 here, they are members of the Virgo Cluster.

understand.summary: This deep image was made with the Burrell Schmidt Telescope in visible light. The packet does not publish the colour mapping.
understand.eye: The halo is far too faint to see by eye; only a very deep image that gathers light for a long time reveals it.

alt: A giant elliptical galaxy with a faint extended halo, surrounded by many other galaxies, including two at top right.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 370, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Just below the centre of this crowded field of galaxies lies a long, stretched feature nicknamed "the Dragon". It is not one object but many duplicated images of a single spiral galaxy far behind the scene. The foreground is the galaxy cluster Abell 370, in the constellation Cetus, roughly four billion light-years away.

The cluster is made of hundreds of galaxies plus dark matter, and all that mass bends and distorts light from objects behind it. Astronomers call this strong gravitational lensing. The cluster acts like an uneven lens, smearing and copying the background spiral into the Dragon, which lies about five billion light-years away.
Abell 370 was the opening target of BUFFALO, a Hubble survey whose aim is to search for some of the very first galaxies in the Universe, using massive clusters like this one as lenses.
explore: Because lensing magnifies as well as distorts, galaxies too faint to detect on their own can be brightened enough for Hubble to see them, which is why survey teams point at massive clusters when hunting for early galaxies.

understand.summary: This image combines data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from visible light into the near-infrared. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Much of this data is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the distant lensed galaxies are far too faint to see without long exposures.

alt: A field full of galaxies of many shapes, with a long, stretched extended feature just below the centre.

caption: The galaxy NGC 4490, the Cocoon Galaxy, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the galaxy NGC 4490, whose shape looks scattered and warped rather than neatly organised. That disorder is the aftermath of a collision with another galaxy, NGC 4485, which lies outside this frame.

Galaxies that pass close to each other pull on one another with tidal forces, gravity that tugs harder on the near side than the far side. Here those forces were extreme. They sculpted both the shape of NGC 4490 and its properties, and they stretched its outer regions out into long extensions.

NGC 4490 was once a barred spiral galaxy, a spiral with a straight bar of stars across its middle. The stretching of its outskirts earned it the nickname the Cocoon Galaxy. Its listed type is a starburst galaxy, one forming stars at a high rate, which fits the picture of a galaxy stirred up by a close encounter.
explore: The image acknowledges D. Calzetti of UMass and the LEGUS Team, together with J. Maund of the University of Sheffield and R. Chandar of the University of Toledo, whose work contributed to it.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from the ultraviolet through visible light, including one that isolates the glow of hydrogen. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet part of this data is invisible to the human eye, and the galaxy itself is far too faint to see this way without a telescope.

alt: A warped, irregular galaxy with scattered, uneven structure.

caption: The interacting galaxies NGC 3169 and NGC 3166, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: Two galaxies sit side by side here: NGC 3169 on the left and NGC 3166 on the right. At the bottom right of the pair, a third galaxy appears, NGC 3165. The picture was taken with the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide Field Imager, at La Silla Observatory in Chile.

The two main galaxies are close enough that each feels the other's gravity, and both carry the scars. They are locked in a gravitational tug of war. In NGC 3169, the spiral shape has been bent out of true, warped by its neighbour's pull.

In NGC 3166 the damage shows in its dust lanes, the dark bands of dust that normally trace a galaxy's structure, which have been broken into fragments. Such interactions are common among galaxies, and over long spans of time they can reshape them completely.
explore: The pair lies about 70 million light-years away in the constellation Sextans. They are classed as an interacting pair, galaxies whose mutual gravity is visibly changing them.

understand.summary: This image was made with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, using blue, visual and red filters in visible light. The packet does not publish the colour mapping.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye can, revealing faint distortions no one could see looking through a telescope.

alt: Two galaxies side by side, a warped spiral on the left and a companion on the right, with a third galaxy at bottom right.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1232 in near-infrared light, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: This is the spiral galaxy NGC 1232, seen in near-infrared light by HAWK-I on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The galaxy sits some 65 million light-years away in Eridanus, the River, and this picture ranks among the sharpest, most detailed views of it ever captured from the ground.

NGC 1232 is classed as an intermediate spiral, halfway between a spiral with a central bar and one without. Near-infrared light passes through dust more easily than visible light and highlights older stars, so a view like this reveals a different side of a galaxy.

There is a bit of history here. A visible-light image of NGC 1232 and its small companion, NGC 1232A, was among the first pictures the Very Large Telescope produced. HAWK-I, among the world's most powerful infrared imagers, returned to the same galaxy to show it in a new light.
explore: The field of view is about 6.4 arcminutes across. Four filters went into the picture, named Y, J, H and K, each capturing a different slice of the near-infrared.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image comes from the HAWK-I camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The Y filter is shown in blue, J in green, H in muddy brown and K in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so these colours are assigned to make it visible.

alt: A spiral galaxy seen in near-infrared light.

caption: The galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403, one of six huge clusters studied by the Hubble Frontier Fields programme. The programme has two goals: to map how mass is spread through these clusters, and to use them as lenses to see deeper into the distant Universe.

A cluster's gravity bends the light of galaxies behind it, magnifying and distorting them. This is gravitational lensing, and the pattern of bent images reveals how much mass the cluster holds, including dark matter that cannot be seen directly.

Researchers used almost 200 images of distant galaxies, bent and magnified by this cluster, together with the depth of Hubble's data. That let them measure the cluster's total mass more precisely than ever before. Each warped background galaxy is a clue, and with enough of them the invisible structure of the cluster comes into focus.
explore: The cluster lies in the constellation Eridanus. Its distance is given as a redshift of 0.396, a measure of how much the expanding Universe has stretched its light on the way to us.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue and visible filters plus one in the near-infrared. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Hubble's long exposures reveal faint, distant galaxies far too dim for the eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A crowded field of galaxies from a massive galaxy cluster.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 83 in infrared light, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: Vast numbers of individual stars fill this infrared view of the nearby galaxy Messier 83. It was made with the HAWK-I camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope, whose sharp image quality combined with the telescope's huge light-collecting power lets the galaxy's stars stand out one by one.

Messier 83 is a spiral galaxy, a flat disc of stars, gas and dust wound into arms around a bright centre. Infrared light can pass through dust that blocks visible light, so views like this help astronomers see stars that would otherwise be hidden.

Building the image took patience. The camera observed three separate infrared bands, and the exposures added up to eight and a half hours. That time was broken into more than five hundred separate exposures, each lasting a single minute, which were then combined into this final picture.
explore: The image spans roughly 13 arcminutes of sky. The galaxy lies roughly 15 million light-years away in the constellation Hydra.

understand.summary: This image was taken with the HAWK-I infrared camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope, in three near-infrared bands, J, H and K. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each band.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and hours of combined exposure collect far more light than an eye ever could.

alt: A spiral galaxy seen in infrared light, filled with countless individual stars.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy Messier 83 in infrared light, imaged at ESO's La Silla Observatory
story: This false-colour infrared photo shows the nearby barred spiral galaxy Messier 83. A barred spiral has a straight band of stars across its centre, from which the spiral arms unwind.

The picture blends three images taken at different infrared wavelengths. Two came from the SOFI instrument on ESO's 3.5-metre New Technology Telescope, and the third from the DFOSC instrument on the Danish 1.54-metre telescope, both at La Silla Observatory in Chile.

The two SOFI images were each built from exposures of four neighbouring fields stitched together into a mosaic. Before combining them, the team subtracted a matching sky frame from every exposure to remove the glow of the sky itself. The third image was reshaped so that its pixels and field of view matched the others, allowing all three to be layered into one picture in which north is up.
explore: The SOFI images were taken in May 2001, while Søren Larsen captured the DFOSC image in February 1998. The final mosaic covers about 9.2 by 8.9 arcminutes of sky.

understand.summary: This infrared composite combines Ks-band and J-band images from SOFI on the New Technology Telescope with an I-band image from DFOSC on the Danish 1.54-metre telescope. Ks is shown in red, J in green and I in blue.
understand.eye: The eye cannot see these infrared wavelengths, so the colours are assigned to represent them.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 6744, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Seen here by Hubble is NGC 6744, a galaxy about 30 million light-years away. The picture blends ultraviolet and visible light, gathered with two of Hubble's cameras, the Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys.

NGC 6744 is one of 50 galaxies observed for the Legacy ExtraGalactic UV Survey, known as LEGUS. It is the sharpest and most thorough ultraviolet survey of star-forming galaxies in the nearby Universe. Ultraviolet light is given off strongly by young, hot stars, so it acts as a tracer of where stars have recently been born.

Combining ultraviolet with visible light lets astronomers compare young stars with older ones in the same galaxy. The survey is meant as a broad resource for understanding star formation and galaxy evolution, two processes that are tightly linked, since the stars a galaxy makes shape how it looks and changes over time.
explore: NGC 6744 lies in the southern constellation Pavo, the Peacock.

understand.summary: This composite uses Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys, with filters spanning ultraviolet and visible light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the human eye, so this image shows light we could never see directly.

alt: A spiral galaxy seen by Hubble in ultraviolet and visible light.

caption: The merging galaxy Arp 220, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: At first glance Arp 220 looks like one strangely shaped galaxy, but it is really the aftermath of two spiral galaxies colliding. The bluish-white bright knots in this Hubble image are huge star clusters, born in a burst of star formation that the collision set off. It sits about 250 million light-years away in the constellation Serpens, the Serpent.

The crash began about 700 million years ago. It has packed roughly 200 giant star clusters into a dusty region only about 5,000 light-years across, around 5 percent of our galaxy's width. Remarkably, that small region holds as much gas as the whole Milky Way.

Arp 220 shines brightest in infrared light, making it an ultraluminous infrared galaxy. Earlier infrared observations peered through the dust and found the cores of the two original galaxies, 1,200 light-years apart. X-rays from both cores, seen by NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, point to two supermassive black holes.
explore: Arp 220 is the brightest of the three galaxy mergers closest to Earth, and it takes its name from being number 220 in Arp's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies.
This picture was one of 59 images of merging galaxies that Hubble released for its 18th anniversary on 24 April 2008.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using a blue filter and a near-infrared filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Much of what makes Arp 220 remarkable is in infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint to view this way without a telescope.

alt: An oddly shaped galaxy with dark dust and bluish-white bright knots of star clusters.

caption: The Meathook Galaxy, NGC 2442, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This wide view takes in the whole of the Meathook Galaxy, NGC 2442, together with the sky around it. Its two spiral arms are clearly lopsided, and the longer one glows pink with intense star formation. The picture comes from the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide Field Imager, at La Silla in Chile.

The pink colour has a simple cause. Young stars pour out radiation that strips electrons from atoms in the gas they formed from, a process called ionisation, and the energised gas then glows. So the pink patches mark where new stars have recently switched on.

Why is the galaxy so uneven? Astronomers think both its lopsided shape and its burst of star formation were caused by tidal forces during a close pass by another galaxy sometime in the past. The gravity of a passing neighbour can distort a galaxy's arms and squeeze its gas into making stars.
explore: This ground-based picture covers far more sky than a Hubble image of the same galaxy, although it shows less fine detail. NGC 2442 lies about 55 million light-years away in the southern constellation Volans.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, with filters including one that isolates the red glow of hydrogen. The packet does not publish the colour mapping.
understand.eye: Long exposures collect far more light than the eye, which could never pick out the faint pink glow of star-forming gas in this galaxy.

alt: A lopsided spiral galaxy with two uneven arms, the longer arm glowing pink, set among surrounding stars.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 66, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view shows Messier 66, a spiral galaxy with an unusual build: its arms are lopsided and its core seems to sit off-centre. It is the biggest of the three interacting spirals known as the Leo Triplet, about 35 million light-years away in the constellation of Leo.

The oddities are most likely the work of gravity. Messier 66 shares its neighbourhood with Messier 65 and NGC 3628, and the pull of these two companions has probably tugged its arms out of shape and shifted its centre. The trio itself belongs to a larger collection of galaxies called the Messier 66 group.

Messier 66 is the biggest of the three, measuring about 100 000 light-years across. Spiral galaxies are often pictured as neat, symmetrical whirls, but galaxies living close together rarely stay tidy, and this one wears the marks of its neighbours plainly.
explore: The three filters used here were combined so that the image represents the galaxy's real colours. One filter captured the glow of hydrogen gas, which highlights regions where stars are forming.

understand.summary: This composite uses Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with a near-infrared filter, a green filter and an H-alpha filter for glowing hydrogen, combined to represent the galaxy's real colours.
understand.eye: Even with realistic colours, the galaxy is far too faint to see in this detail by eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light the eye cannot detect.

alt: A spiral galaxy with uneven, lopsided arms and an off-centre core.

caption: The dwarf galaxy NGC 4214, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A huge glowing cloud of hydrogen gas dominates much of this galaxy, and at its centre sits a heart-shaped hollow. This is NGC 4214, pictured with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, which was the telescope's newest camera when the image was made.

The glowing cloud is a nursery where new stars are forming, which makes the galaxy an ideal place to study how stars are born and how they evolve. Inside the heart-shaped cavity is a large cluster of massive young stars, with temperatures from 10 000 to 50 000 degrees Celsius.

Those stars carved the hollow themselves. Their strong stellar winds, streams of particles blowing off their surfaces, pushed the gas outward into a bubble. That has a side effect: with the gas cleared away, the raw material for making more stars is gone, so the same winds that shaped the heart are also slowing further star birth nearby.
explore: NGC 4214 is a dwarf galaxy, much smaller than the Milky Way, lying about 10 million light-years away in the constellation Canes Venatici.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from the ultraviolet through visible light to the near-infrared, including ones tuned to glowing hydrogen and oxygen. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the galaxy is far too faint to see in this detail without a large telescope.

alt: A galaxy dominated by a glowing cloud of gas with a heart-shaped hollow at its centre.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4522, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Though this is a still image, the spiral galaxy NGC 4522 almost seems to swirl, with ghostly gas being driven out of it. Bright blue pockets of newborn stars sit to the right and left of centre. The galaxy lies some 60 million light-years away, in the Virgo galaxy cluster.

NGC 4522 is being stripped of its gas right now. It races through the cluster so fast, an estimated 10 million kilometres per hour or more, that it meets a strong wind from the thin, hot gas that fills the cluster. That wind pushes the galaxy's own gas out behind it, a process called ram pressure stripping.

The effect is powerful enough to mangle galaxies and even shut down their star formation, since gas is the fuel stars are made from. Oddly, some of the stripped gas has formed new star clusters of its own, and several of them are visible in this Hubble picture.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys gives astronomers a detailed view of ram pressure stripping in action, including the newly formed star clusters that developed in the gas torn from the galaxy.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The faint streams of stripped gas are far too dim for the eye; they only show up in Hubble's long exposures.

alt: A spiral galaxy with wispy gas being forced out of it and bright blue patches of new stars to the right and left of centre.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 370, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view of the galaxy cluster Abell 370 is full of arcs and streaks. They are the stretched images of galaxies lying far behind the cluster, their light bent on its way to us. The cluster itself is some five billion light-years away.

Abell 370 was one of the very first clusters where astronomers saw this effect, called gravitational lensing. The cluster's gravity warps spacetime, the fabric of space and time, and light passing through that warped region is bent and distorted, much as a curved glass lens reshapes what is seen through it.

This picture marks an ending. It came from the final observation of the Frontier Fields programme. With this last look at Abell 370, one of the first places where lensing was ever seen, the programme came to a close.
explore: Lensed images carry information both ways: they magnify faint background galaxies, and their shapes reveal how the cluster's mass, including unseen dark matter, is spread out.

understand.summary: This image combines data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, with filters from visible light into the near-infrared. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The near-infrared part of the data is invisible to the eye, and the faint background galaxies need Hubble's long exposures to appear at all.

caption: The Leo Triplet and surrounding field, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Three bright galaxies in Leo, the Lion, sit in this wide view, surrounded by a crowd of fainter objects. Some of those fainter points are distant galaxies far in the background, while others are much closer stars in our own Milky Way.

The trio is known as the Leo Triplet, a group of interacting galaxies about 35 million light-years away. The picture was made with the VLT Survey Telescope and its OmegaCAM camera, and it shows why this pairing is suited to wide surveys.

Survey telescopes like this one cover large areas of sky at once. That makes them good at mapping the Universe beyond our galaxy, and at picking up very faint, low-brightness structures in the Milky Way's halo, the sparse region of stars that surrounds its disc. A single frame like this holds nearby stars, galaxies in the middle distance and faint galaxies far beyond.
explore: The image is a composite of exposures through three different filters, each given its own colour so that the combined picture shows how the scene looks across visible and near-infrared light.

understand.summary: This composite comes from the OmegaCAM camera on the VLT Survey Telescope. Light through a near-infrared filter is coloured red, light from the red part of the spectrum is coloured green, and green light is coloured magenta.

caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 273, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows Arp 273, a pair of galaxies caught interacting. The larger of the two has a distorted shape, bearing clear signs of tidal interactions with its smaller companion.

Tidal interactions happen when galaxies pass close enough for gravity to pull unevenly on them, stretching and bending their structure. In this case astronomers think the encounter was more intimate than a close pass: the smaller galaxy is thought to have actually passed through the larger one. Galaxies are mostly empty space between their stars, so such a crossing does not mean stars smash together, but it can badly disturb the shape of both galaxies.

The picture was released to celebrate 21 years since Hubble was launched. The pair lies about 300 million light-years away in the constellation Andromeda, their encounter frozen for a moment in this single frame.
explore: The image was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, which was used to capture ultraviolet, blue and red light from the pair.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters in ultraviolet, blue and red light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is ultraviolet light, which the eye cannot see, and the pair is far too faint to see this way without a large telescope.

alt: A pair of interacting galaxies, the larger one distorted in shape beside its smaller companion.

caption: The irregular galaxy NGC 4485, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the galaxy NGC 4485. Off to its right runs a stream of bright knots, huge pockets of gas and enormous star-forming regions, where young, massive blue stars are being born. Below the galaxy sits a bright orange galaxy far in the background.

NGC 4485 was once an orderly spiral. A dramatic gravitational encounter with its larger neighbour, NGC 4490, which lies out of frame to the bottom right, wrecked that structure and turned it into an irregular galaxy.

The same interaction drew out the stream, about 25 000 light-years long, which links the two galaxies. Its bright knots, huge pockets of gas and star-forming regions are all products of that same dramatic gravitational interplay between the two neighbours.
explore: The orange background galaxy gives off X-rays that have been studied with the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and it lies about 850 million light-years from Earth, far beyond NGC 4485.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, with filters from the ultraviolet through visible light to the near-infrared, plus one for glowing hydrogen. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and these faint features need Hubble's long exposures.

alt: An irregular galaxy with a stream of bright knots and blue star-forming regions to its right and an orange background galaxy below.

caption: The galaxy ESO 137-001, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory
story: Electric blue streaks pour out of the galaxy ESO 137-001 in this image, and a giant stream of gas stretches toward the bottom of the frame. The picture combines Hubble observations with X-ray data from NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory.

The blue streaks are the signature of ram pressure stripping. As a galaxy moves through the hot, thin gas between galaxies in a cluster, that gas pushes against it like a headwind, and the galaxy's own gas is blown out behind it.

The large stream toward the bottom of the frame can only be seen in X-rays. It is gas that has been heated to very high temperatures, glowing at wavelengths no ordinary camera can capture. By pairing Hubble's view with Chandra's, astronomers can trace both the visible streaks and the much hotter gas that the galaxy is losing.
explore: ESO 137-001 lies about 200 million light-years away in the southern constellation Triangulum Australe.

understand.summary: This composite pairs visible and near-infrared images from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with X-ray data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each dataset.
understand.eye: X-rays are invisible to the eye, so the giant gas stream would not be visible at all without Chandra.

alt: A galaxy with electric blue streaks trailing from it and a giant stream of gas extending toward the bottom of the frame.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 6744, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This is NGC 6744, a large, nearby spiral galaxy photographed with the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide Field Imager, at La Silla in Chile. What makes it special is its resemblance to our own galaxy.

We can never photograph the Milky Way from outside, because we live inside its disc. NGC 6744 is similar enough that this image works almost like a picture postcard of home, as if someone had mailed us a snapshot of our galaxy from far out in intergalactic space.

A spiral galaxy like this one is a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust, with arms winding out from a brighter centre. The picture was built from four exposures. Three captured blue, yellow-green and red light, and a fourth isolated the glow of hydrogen gas, which traces regions where new stars are forming. Together they show both the galaxy's starlight and its active nurseries.
explore: NGC 6744 lies about 30 million light-years away in the southern constellation Pavo, the Peacock.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope. Blue light is shown as blue, yellow-green as green, red as orange, and the glow of hydrogen gas as red.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see this way by eye; the long exposures gather much more light than an eye can.

alt: A large spiral galaxy with arms winding out from a bright centre.

caption: The galaxy cluster MACSJ1720+35, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the heart of a vast galaxy cluster called MACSJ1720+35, seen in visible and near-infrared light. In the top right, just barely visible, is an exploding star nicknamed Caracalla, which lies behind the cluster.

The cluster's mass is so great that its gravity warps, brightens and enlarges the light of objects behind it, an effect called gravitational lensing. Caracalla is a Type Ia supernova, a kind of stellar explosion that astronomers value because it reaches a consistent peak brightness, which makes it useful for estimating distances.

That combination is valuable. Because astronomers know how bright a Type Ia supernova should be, a lensed one lets them check how strongly the cluster is magnifying things, testing the optical prescription of the cluster lens. Caracalla was one of three exploding stars found in the CLASH survey with Hubble.
explore: CLASH, the Cluster Lensing And Supernova survey with Hubble, charted how dark matter is spread through 25 galaxy clusters. Dark matter is invisible, yet it is believed to account for most of the matter in the Universe.
Follow-up observations of Caracalla came from a Hubble programme run by the Supernova Cosmology Project.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters from visible light into the near-infrared. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the faint supernova behind the cluster needed Hubble's long exposures to show up at all.

alt: The crowded centre of a galaxy cluster, with a faint supernova just visible in the top right.

caption: The merging galaxy NGC 2623, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two long tails of young stars stretch out from a single bright centre in this Hubble image of NGC 2623. The galaxy is the product of a merger that is now in its late stages: the cores of the two original galaxies have already combined into one nucleus.

When galaxies approach one another, studies show that large amounts of gas are pulled from each toward the other's centre, until the pair eventually fuses into one large galaxy. The tidal tails are a strong sign that such a merger has happened, and the violent exchange of gas and mass has set off star formation in both tails.

The lower tail stands out. It is rich in bright star clusters, and 100 of them turned up in these observations. They may have formed in a loop of stretched material linked to the northern tail, or from debris falling back onto the nucleus.
explore: Beyond that busy lower tail, both of the galaxy's arms host very young stars that are only in the early stages of their lives. NGC 2623 lies about 300 million light-years away in the constellation Cancer.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 100, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: This is Messier 100, a spiral galaxy about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. The picture was made with the FORS1 instrument on Kueyen, one of the telescopes that make up ESO's Very Large Telescope.

It is a composite of five separate images, each taken through a different filter. Four of them, named U, V, R and I, capture broad slices of light from the ultraviolet edge of the spectrum through visible light to the near-infrared. The fifth is a narrow filter that picks out the H-alpha line, the red glow of hydrogen gas, which highlights regions where new stars are being born.

The exposures were short by astronomical standards. The V, R and I images each took 60 seconds, the U image 3 minutes and the hydrogen image 5 minutes. The picture covers a patch of sky 6.8 by 5.1 arcminutes, with north at the top.
explore: The images were taken by Dominique Naef, Eric Depagne and Chris Lidman of ESO, and the final processing was carried out by Kristina Boneva, Haennes Heyer and Henri Boffin.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1365 in infrared light, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: This infrared image shows NGC 1365, a barred spiral galaxy, photographed with the powerful HAWK-I infrared camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile.

A barred spiral is a spiral galaxy with a straight band of stars running across its centre, with the spiral arms trailing from the ends of the bar. NGC 1365 is a member of the Fornax galaxy cluster, roughly 60 million light-years from Earth.

Infrared light passes through much of the dust that blocks visible light, so an infrared view like this one reveals the stars and structure of a galaxy in a different way than an ordinary photograph. The picture was assembled from images taken through four filters, called Y, J, H and K, each sensitive to a different slice of infrared light. Exposures lasted 4, 4, 7 and 12 minutes in turn, and the four were combined into this single view.

story: This is NGC 55, an irregular galaxy photographed with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile. Unlike spirals or ellipticals, an irregular galaxy has no clear, orderly shape.

NGC 55 is about 7.5 million light-years away, which makes it a relatively close neighbour in galactic terms, and it measures some 70,000 light-years across. It lies in the southern constellation Sculptor.

The image was built from data taken through three filters. Two of them, called B and V, capture blue and yellow-green visible light, showing the galaxy's starlight. The third, H-alpha, isolates the red glow given off by hydrogen gas, and so highlights clouds where stars are forming. The field of view is 30 arcminutes wide, with north at the top and east to the left.

caption: The centre of the Milky Way, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This infrared image from Hubble looks toward the centre of our own galaxy, the Milky Way, 27,000 light-years from Earth. In ordinary visible light, this region is hidden behind thick clouds of dust.

Infrared light can slip through that dust, which is why astronomers used Hubble's infrared capabilities to peer into the region. What they see is a nuclear star cluster, a dense crowd of stars packed around the very middle of the galaxy.

At the centre of that cluster, and at the centre of this image, lies the Milky Way's supermassive black hole, known as Sagittarius A*. A supermassive black hole is an object so dense that not even light can escape it, and one of these is thought to sit at the heart of most large galaxies. The black hole itself cannot be seen, but the crowded stars around it show how busy our galaxy's core really is.
explore: The Galactic Centre lies in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius, which is why its black hole carries that name.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3344, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This is the spiral galaxy NGC 3344, which lies about 20 million light-years from Earth. The picture merges images shot through seven separate filters with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3.

Those filters cover a broad range of light, from the ultraviolet through the visible part of the spectrum and on into the near-infrared. Each wavelength range picks out something different in a galaxy. Ultraviolet light tends to come from young, hot stars, visible light shows the overall population of stars, and near-infrared light helps to reveal older stars and see through some of the dust.

Combining them produces a detailed portrait. It also gives astronomers a way to study many aspects of the galaxy at once, from where stars are forming to how its older population is spread out. NGC 3344 lies in the constellation Leo Minor.

caption: The grand design spiral galaxy Messier 81, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The arms of Messier 81, a large grand design spiral galaxy, wind all the way down into its centre in this Hubble image. When it was released, it was the sharpest image ever taken of this galaxy.
A grand design spiral has long, well-defined arms that sweep neatly around the galaxy. Messier 81 is a spiral of stars, dust and clouds of gas, and it lies 11.6 million light-years away.

Even at that distance, Hubble's view is sharp enough to pick out individual stars. It also resolves open star clusters, which are loose groups of young stars, and globular clusters, which are dense balls of old stars. It even shows glowing patches of fluorescent gas, lit up by nearby stars. The image was built from blue, visible and infrared light.
explore: The picture was first presented at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society in Honolulu, Hawaii. Messier 81 lies in the constellation Ursa Major.

caption: The galaxies NGC 1316 and NGC 1317, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: Two galaxies with very different histories share this picture from the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. The larger one is NGC 1316, and on the right is its smaller companion, NGC 1317.
Their contrast is the point. NGC 1317 appears to have lived a quiet, peaceful life. NGC 1316, by comparison, carries the scars of earlier mergers with other galaxies.

Galaxies grow partly by absorbing their neighbours. When one galaxy swallows another, the collision can scramble the larger galaxy's shape and leave behind disturbed features that last for a long time afterward. Seen side by side, this pair shows two possible paths: a galaxy that has been left alone, and one whose past has been shaped by repeated encounters. Both lie about 60 million light-years away, in the constellation Fornax.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, using blue, visual and red filters plus an H-alpha filter for glowing hydrogen. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, which could never pick out the faint scars of past mergers directly.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell S1063, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A bright-white elliptical galaxy sits at the centre of this field, the core of the galaxy cluster Abell S1063. Around it curl short red arcs, the images of far more distant galaxies, magnified and warped. A couple of foreground stars shine large and bright, each with Webb's signature eight-point spikes.

Galaxy clusters are among the most massive objects in the Universe, and their gravity bends light passing near them, an effect called gravitational lensing. Webb was observing this cluster for a different purpose when, by luck, it also caught a little red dot later named GLIMPSE-17775.

GLIMPSE-17775 belongs to a class of objects that astronomers call little red dots. Lensing, combined with 30 hours of Webb observing time, let scientists record the deepest spectrum yet of one of them. It gave the strongest evidence so far for a hot, dense cocoon of gas known as a "black hole star".
explore: A spectrum spreads an object's light out by wavelength, revealing what it is made of and how it behaves. Getting a deep one of such a faint object depends on both long observing time and the natural magnification that the cluster provides.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image comes from Webb's NIRCam. The shortest wavelengths, from 900 nm to 1.5 micrometres, are shown in blue, those around 2.0 to 2.77 micrometres in green, and the longest, 3.56 to 4.44 micrometres, in red.

caption: The merging galaxies Arp 256, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two spiral galaxies with badly bent shapes fill this Hubble image, scattered with a huge number of blue star-forming knots that look a little like bursting fireworks. This is Arp 256, a system about 350 million light-years away in the constellation Cetus.

The pair is in an early stage of merging. As the two galaxies pass close to each other, their gravity pulls and twists them out of their original spiral forms, which is why their shapes are so distorted.

The blue knots are the most striking consequence. The close interaction between the galaxies has triggered a wave of star formation, compressing gas and setting off the birth of many new, hot stars that glow blue. Over time the two galaxies are expected to settle into one, but for now they are caught mid-collision.
explore: This picture, from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, is a new version of an image first released in 2008. That earlier image was part of a collection of 59 pictures of merging galaxies made for Hubble's 18th anniversary.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4921, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy NGC 4921 sits in front of a rich backdrop of more distant galaxies in this very deep Hubble image. It belongs to the Coma Galaxy Cluster and lies about 250 million light-years away, in the constellation Coma Berenices.

A deep image is one that gathers light for a very long time, letting faint objects appear that a short exposure would miss. This one was assembled from a total of 80 separate pictures, taken through yellow and near-infrared filters and then combined.

The result shows two things at once. In the foreground is NGC 4921 itself, which astronomers describe as an unusual spiral. Behind it, across the rest of the frame, the long exposure picks up galaxies much farther away, each a system of stars in its own right, reduced by distance to small smudges and specks of light.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, built from yellow and near-infrared filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 300 in hydrogen light, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This view of the spiral galaxy NGC 300 was taken through a narrow filter that lets through only the red light of hydrogen atoms, known as H-alpha. It picks out clouds of glowing gas rather than the full starlight of the galaxy.

Many of those clouds owe their shapes to a population of bright young stars that switched on just a few million years ago. Their intense radiation and strong stellar winds, streams of particles flowing off their surfaces, have sculpted the surrounding gas. The radiation also strips electrons from the hydrogen, and this ionised gas forms shells, known as HII shells, that glow in the image.

Not everything here is in space. The rings visible around some of the bright stars are not real structures at all; they are caused by internal reflections inside the telescope, a reminder that every picture carries a trace of the instrument that took it.
explore: NGC 300 lies about 6 million light-years away in the southern constellation Sculptor.

understand.summary: This image was taken with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope through a single H-alpha filter, which isolates the red glow of hydrogen.
understand.eye: A narrow filter shows only one colour of light, so this view isolates hydrogen gas in a way the eye, which takes in all visible colours at once, cannot.

caption: The elliptical galaxy PGC 6240, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Delicate, petal-like shells surround the galaxy PGC 6240 in this detailed Hubble image, set against a sky crowded with far-off galaxies. PGC 6240 is an elliptical galaxy, a smooth, rounded collection of stars, lying about 350 million light-years away in the southern constellation Hydrus, the Water Snake.
The galaxy is orbited by a number of globular clusters, dense balls of stars, and they contain a mix of young and old stars. That is unusual, since globular clusters are typically made of old stars.

Astronomers think the mixture comes from a galaxy merger that happened fairly recently. In that picture, the young clusters are a record of the encounter, a sign that this elliptical galaxy has not always led a quiet life.
explore: Judy Schmidt is credited in the image's acknowledgement. The picture was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through a blue filter and a near-infrared filter.

story: This is the spiral galaxy NGC 3621, photographed with the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope's Wide Field Imager at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. It lies about 22 million light-years away, in Hydra, the Sea Snake.

NGC 3621 is comparatively bright for a galaxy, so it can be seen well even through moderate-sized telescopes. Like other spirals, it is a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust, arranged in arms around a brighter centre.

The image has an unusual origin. Its data were not taken for this picture specifically, but already sat in the ESO archive, where Joe DePasquale picked them out for the Hidden Treasures competition. Archives like ESO's hold enormous amounts of observations, and competitions like this one encouraged people to dig through them and turn raw data into finished pictures.

caption: The galaxy NGC 6503, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the galaxy NGC 6503, which lies about 18 million light-years away in the constellation Draco. It is classed as a spiral galaxy and as a dwarf, smaller than giants like the Milky Way.

What makes NGC 6503 unusual is its surroundings. It sits at the edge of a strangely empty region of space called the Local Void. Galaxies across the Universe are arranged in a web of clusters and filaments, and voids are the large gaps in between, where very few galaxies are found.

This newer view shows a very rich set of colours that adds detail to earlier images of the galaxy. It combines filters from the ultraviolet, through visible light, and into the near-infrared, along with one that isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, often a sign of star-forming regions.

caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 142, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two galaxies are caught interacting in this Hubble image, and together they look strikingly like a penguin watching over its egg. The pair is known as Arp 142, and it lies about 400 million light-years away in the constellation Hydra.

The penguin is NGC 2936, which was once a standard spiral galaxy. The pull of its neighbour has twisted it out of its original shape. The egg is NGC 2937, a smaller elliptical galaxy, a smooth rounded collection of stars.

Interactions like this are a normal part of galaxy life. Gravity between two galaxies passing close to each other can stretch spirals into strange forms, pull out streams of stars and gas, and sometimes, over long stretches of time, lead to a full merger. For now, this pair offers a snapshot of a galaxy in the middle of being reshaped.
explore: The image combines visible and infrared light gathered by Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3.

caption: The Meathook Galaxy, NGC 2442, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: In this close-up, Hubble zooms in on the Meathook Galaxy, NGC 2442, focusing on its central regions and the more compact of its two lopsided spiral arms. The galaxy lies about 55 million light-years away in the southern constellation Volans.

That arm has a history. In 1999, a supernova exploded there, the bright death of a star. Hubble made these observations in 2006 specifically to study what the explosion left behind. A supernova can briefly outshine an entire galaxy, and looking back at the site years later helps astronomers learn about the star that exploded and its surroundings.

To complete the frame, parts of the image's edges were filled in with ground-based data from the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, so the picture blends observations from space and from Chile's La Silla site.
explore: The supernova is catalogued as SN 1999ga, a name that records the year it was discovered.

caption: The centre of the Milky Way in infrared light, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: Thousands of individual stars crowd this infrared view of the centre of our Milky Way, in the southern constellation Sagittarius, the Archer. Their colours tell their temperatures, with blue stars hot and red stars cool, and between them glows infrared light from dust.

The galactic centre is "only" 26,000 light-years away, close enough that sharp images can pick out stars within the central region, just one light-year wide. By tracking how those stars move, astronomers can measure the gravity that steers them.

Over about a decade, those measurements showed that roughly 3 million times the mass of the Sun is packed within just 10 light-days of a compact radio and X-ray source called Sagittarius A*. That makes it the most likely match for the black hole believed to sit at the heart of our galaxy.
explore: The picture was made with the NACO instrument on the 8.2-metre VLT Yepun telescope, combining frames taken in three infrared bands spanning 1.6 to 3.5 micrometres. A newer image of the same region was published in 2008.

caption: Part of the galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Galaxies of every shape and colour glow against black space here: large blue spirals, big pale-white ellipticals, and many medium-sized orange and red galaxies, down to tiny faint specks. This is part of the galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223, seen by Webb's Near-Infrared Camera, NIRCam.

Webb's sensitivity to infrared light, and hours of combined exposure, pull distant galaxies, shown in red, out of the darkness. The image covers a "parallel field", a neighbouring area of the cluster observed alongside its crowded centre, as part of the CANUCS survey of massive clusters.

In this very field, researchers found a far-off galaxy called CANUCS-LRD-z8.6, seen as it was only 570 million years after the Big Bang. Its central supermassive black hole is surprisingly big for so early a time, a finding that challenges current ideas about how galaxies and black holes first formed.
explore: The CANUCS survey used Webb's NIRCam, NIRISS and NIRSpec instruments to gather infrared images and spectra of massive galaxy clusters. That let astronomers study low-mass galaxies in these clusters at early stages of their development.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 7469, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A spiral galaxy with blue-purple hues and orange-red star-filled regions spreads across this image, with a bright centre crossed by a large star-shaped pattern. This is NGC 7469, a luminous, face-on spiral about 90 000 light-years wide, some 220 million light-years away in Pegasus. Its companion, IC 5283, peeks in at lower left.

The star shape is not a star. It is a diffraction spike pattern, made as light from the galaxy's bright core bends around the edges of Webb's hexagonal mirror segments and the strut holding its secondary mirror.

That core is an active galactic nucleus, blazing as gas and dust fall toward a central black hole. A ring of intense star formation circles it just 1,500 light-years out. Webb has found very young star clusters never seen before, warm turbulent gas, and signs that the nucleus is destroying small dust grains nearby.
explore: Highly ionised gas appears to be streaming out of the nucleus at about 6.4 million kilometres an hour, part of a known galactic outflow now seen in much finer detail.
The work is part of the GOALS programme, which examines four nearby merging luminous infrared galaxies to learn about star formation, black hole growth and feedback.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1073, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 1073, a barred spiral galaxy in the constellation of Cetus, the Sea Monster. It lies about 55 million light-years away.
A barred spiral is a spiral galaxy with a straight band of stars across its middle, and the spiral arms wind outward from the ends of that bar.

NGC 1073 has a special interest for us. The Milky Way, our home galaxy, is also thought to be a barred spiral. Because we sit inside the Milky Way's disc, we can never step outside to see its overall shape. Studying galaxies like NGC 1073 from the outside gives astronomers a way to learn more about the structure of our own celestial home, using a similar galaxy as a stand-in for the one we cannot photograph.

caption: The Triangulum Galaxy, Messier 33, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Millions of stars, hundreds of clusters of stars and glowing nebulae fill this enormous mosaic of the Triangulum Galaxy, also called Messier 33. It covers the galaxy's central region and inner spiral arms, and it is so large that it is best explored with a zoom tool rather than viewed all at once.

The picture was stitched together from about 54 separate pointings of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Its full size is 34 372 by 19 345 pixels, making it the second-largest image Hubble has ever released. Only Hubble's earlier portrait of the Andromeda Galaxy is bigger.

The Triangulum Galaxy is a spiral about 3 million light-years away. At that distance Hubble can separate individual stars, so the mosaic works as a detailed census, letting astronomers study how stars, clusters and gas clouds are spread across a whole galaxy.
explore: Nebulae are clouds of gas and dust, and the bright ones scattered through this mosaic are often places where stars are forming.

understand.summary: This mosaic comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using a blue-green filter and a near-infrared filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.

caption: The merging galaxies NGC 5256, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Streamers of gas surround the two nuclei in this Hubble image, and blue spiral trails mark places where stars have recently formed. This is NGC 5256, also called Markarian 266, a pair of disc galaxies on the verge of merging, about 350 million light-years away in Ursa Major, the Great Bear.

The whole system is badly disturbed, and observations in infrared, millimetre-wave and radio light add evidence of a starburst, a burst of star formation. Each galaxy also holds an active galactic nucleus, a sign that the turmoil is letting gas fall toward their central black holes while also feeding new stars.
X-rays add another layer. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory found that both nuclei, and a region of hot gas between them, have been heated by shock waves as gas clouds slam together at high speed.
explore: This picture belongs to a collection of 59 images of merging galaxies that Hubble released for its 18th anniversary on 24 April 2008.

caption: The giant elliptical galaxy NGC 4874 in the Coma Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The brightest object here, on the right, is NGC 4874, a star-like core wrapped in a hazy halo. Other cluster galaxies float around it like flying saucers. Look closer and the space around it is peppered with points of light, almost all of them globular clusters, each holding many hundreds of thousands of stars.

Sitting at the heart of the Coma Galaxy Cluster, NGC 4874 is a giant elliptical galaxy roughly ten times the size of the Milky Way. Its strong gravity holds onto more than 30 000 globular clusters, more than any other galaxy we know of.

A few of those points turned out to be something else: ultra-compact dwarf galaxies, only about 200 light-years across and mostly made of old stars. Astronomers think they are the leftover cores of small elliptical galaxies that were stripped of their gas and outer stars in violent encounters within the cluster.
explore: Small smudges in the background are galaxies far beyond the cluster, whose light spent anywhere from several hundred million to billions of years travelling to us. The Coma galaxies themselves are about 350 million light-years away.
A faint blue satellite trail crosses the whole frame from upper left to lower right, a rare sight because Hubble sees only a tiny patch of sky at once.

caption: The Needle Galaxy, IC 2233, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A thin sliver of light cuts across this Hubble image, tinged bluish along its length. This is IC 2233, a spiral galaxy seen edge-on and one of the flattest galaxies known, like a silver needle in a haystack of space.

Most spirals, including the Milky Way, have three main visible parts: a disc containing the spiral arms along with most of the gas and dust, a sparse halo around it, and a central bulge packed with ancient stars. IC 2233 is a super-thin galaxy, at least ten times wider than it is thick, and like almost all such galaxies it has a low brightness and no bulge at all.

The bluish tint along the disc gives away its spiral nature, pointing to hot, bright young stars born from clouds of gas. Unusually, it has no well-defined dust lane, only a few small patches near its middle.
explore: IC 2233 lies in the constellation Lynx, about 40 million light-years away, and was first found in 1894 by the British astronomer Isaac Roberts.
A version of this image was entered into Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition by Luca Limatola.

caption: The core of the Cigar Galaxy, Messier 82, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Glowing gas and dark dust lanes dominate this view of the core of Messier 82, the Cigar Galaxy, while its stars appear faint. It was the most detailed image ever made of this starburst galaxy, which lies about 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major, the Great Bear.

Earlier Hubble pictures showed Messier 82 blazing with stars. The difference comes from the filters. Hubble's cameras record only in greyscale, and colour images are built by combining exposures taken through different filters.

Broad filters, close to the colours our eyes see, give natural-looking images with bright stars. The filters used here instead pass only the light given off by particular chemical elements. That isolates the glowing gas clouds and blocks much of the starlight, so the stars fade and the dust lanes stand out sharply against the bright gas.
explore: Messier 82 is rich in dust, young stars and glowing gas, and it is both unusually bright and fairly close to Earth. The field of view is about 2.7 by 2.7 arcminutes.

caption: The spiral galaxy UGC 2885, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows UGC 2885, a spiral galaxy that could be the biggest in the local universe. It lies 232 million light-years away in the northern constellation of Perseus.

Its size is hard to picture. UGC 2885 measures 2.5 times the width of our Milky Way, which is itself a large galaxy, and it holds 10 times as many stars. The word "may" matters here: the title of largest is a possibility rather than a settled record.

A spiral galaxy is a flattened, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust, arranged in arms that wind out from a brighter centre. If that title holds, UGC 2885 marks the upper end of how large a galaxy in our part of the Universe can grow, which is what makes this portrait of it so striking to study.

caption: The dwarf galaxy NGC 4449, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hundreds of thousands of vivid blue and red stars fill this Hubble image of the galaxy NGC 4449. Hot, bluish-white clusters of massive stars are scattered throughout, mixed with many dustier, reddish regions where stars are forming right now. Huge dark clouds of gas and dust stand out in silhouette against the bright starlight.
NGC 4449 is a dwarf galaxy, far smaller than the Milky Way, lying about 12 million light-years away in the constellation Canes Venatici.

The colours carry meaning. Blue-white clusters are made of hot, massive, young stars, which burn brightly but live short lives, while the reddish, dusty patches mark places where new stars are still being born. The dark clouds are the raw material, gas and dust that may one day collapse into stars of their own. Together they show a small galaxy that is busy making stars across its whole body.

caption: The Southern Pinwheel Galaxy, Messier 83, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Bright stars and thick dust are scattered throughout this Hubble image of the spiral galaxy Messier 83, also known as the Southern Pinwheel Galaxy. It lies about 15 million light-years away in the constellation Hydra.

Messier 83 is a barred spiral, one with a straight band of stars across its centre from which its arms unwind, and it is among the largest and closest barred spirals to us. That combination of size and nearness makes it an appealing target, since astronomers can study its structure in fine detail.

The galaxy also holds some puzzles. Many supernova explosions, the violent deaths of stars, have gone off within it. And at its core there appears to be a double nucleus, two concentrations rather than one, a feature astronomers are still working to understand.

caption: The spiral galaxy ESO 137-001, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Intense blue streaks stream outward from the spiral galaxy ESO 137-001 in this Hubble image, shining brightly in ultraviolet light. The galaxy is framed against a bright background as it travels through the heart of the galaxy cluster Abell 3627.

Those streaks are hot, wispy streams of gas that the galaxy's surroundings are ripping away from it. The space inside a cluster is not empty; it is filled with thin, hot gas. As the galaxy moves through it, that gas pushes back like a strong wind.

The process is called ram pressure stripping, a drag force felt by any object moving through a fluid, similar to what you feel pushing a hand through water. For a galaxy, the effect can be severe. Gas is the raw material for new stars, so losing it this way can eventually starve the galaxy of the fuel it needs to keep forming them.
explore: ESO 137-001 lies about 220 million light-years away in the southern constellation Triangulum Australe.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 1689, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Arc-shaped objects curve around the galaxy cluster Abell 1689 in this Hubble image. They are galaxies located far behind the cluster, their light bent and stretched on the way to us.

The cluster contains a trillion stars, and their combined gravity acts like a zoom lens. Light from distant galaxies passing near the cluster is bent and magnified, an effect called gravitational lensing.

The magnification is the useful part. Because the lensed galaxies appear brighter and larger than they otherwise would, astronomers can study remote galaxies in far greater detail than they could without the cluster's help. In effect, the Universe has provided a natural telescope, and Hubble looks through it to see objects too faint to study on their own.
explore: The cluster's distance is listed as a redshift of 0.183, a measure of how much the expansion of the Universe has stretched its light.

caption: The ring galaxy NGC 922, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: An almost complete circle of bright pink nebulae runs around a spiral galaxy in this Hubble image of NGC 922. The pink ring and the galaxy's twisted spiral shape both trace back to a single dramatic event.

Some 330 million years ago, a smaller galaxy scored a cosmic bullseye, plunging right through the centre of NGC 922. A collision like this sends a disturbance rippling outward through the larger galaxy's disc, like a stone dropped into a pond, and it bends the galaxy out of its original form.

The pink colour marks nebulae, clouds of gas lit up by young stars. As the ripple moves outward, it compresses gas and sets off star formation, which is why the ring is lined with glowing clouds. Galaxies shaped this way are known as ring galaxies, and NGC 922 is a clear example of how they form.
explore: NGC 922 lies about 150 million light-years away in the constellation Fornax.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 5584, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view shows the spiral galaxy NGC 5584, in the constellation of Virgo. It played a key part in a study that measured how fast the Universe is expanding more precisely than ever before.

Hubble resolves the galaxy into thousands of separate stars. Some of them are Cepheids, bright stars that pulse in brightness. Once you know how long a Cepheid takes to brighten and fade, you can work out how bright it truly is. Comparing that with how bright it looks reveals its distance, the most accurate way to measure distances to most nearby galaxies.

A team led by Adam Riess used Cepheids in several galaxies to pin down the expansion rate, known as Hubble's constant, to an accuracy of 3.3 percent. NGC 5584 also recently hosted a Type Ia supernova, a kind of explosion used to measure the far Universe, making it a valuable link between the two distance scales.
explore: The galaxy was first spotted as a faint glow by the visual observer E. E. Barnard in 1881, using only a 12.5-cm telescope.
The image was built from many exposures totalling 20.8 hours, and covers a field 2.4 arcminutes across.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4945 and surrounding sky, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This wide field is centred on the spiral galaxy NGC 4945. Around it, faint, slightly red patches are much more distant galaxies, and most of the point-like sources are stars in our own Milky Way. A good number of the points near NGC 4945, though, are globular clusters belonging to the galaxy itself.

Globular clusters are dense, ball-shaped groups of old stars that orbit galaxies. Picking them out among foreground stars requires a sharp image, and this one resolves about 1 arcsecond, which corresponds to roughly 62 light-years at the galaxy's distance, given here as 13 million light-years.

The photo was made with the Wide-Field-Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, during the camera's early testing phase. It was assembled from 14 CCD frames, together recording more than 70 x 10 9 photons, and it covers a patch of sky 32 by 32 arcminutes.
explore: The red filter was very narrow, and because of how fast NGC 4945 is moving away from us, it does not capture the galaxy's glowing hydrogen emission. Each frame recorded 67,076,064 pixels.

story: We see the galaxy NGC 7090 edge-on in this Hubble image, so its spiral arms are hard to make out. Instead, the view shows its disc and bulging central core, with an intricate pattern of pinkish-red patches spread across the whole galaxy and dark dust lanes inside the disc.
The pink regions are clouds of hydrogen gas, and they mark places where stars are forming right now. They offer visual confirmation of studies that class NGC 7090 as an actively star-forming galaxy.

The dark lanes are dust, mostly in the lower half, with a fine, threadlike structure. Looking through the whole disc from outside, the dust soaks up light from the bright centre and stands out in silhouette. Dust like this is a long-standing obstacle for astronomers, but near-infrared light passes through it largely unhindered, and radio telescopes can observe the dust itself.
explore: NGC 7090 lies in the southern constellation Indus, the Indian, about thirty million light-years from the Sun according to the caption. John Herschel first observed it on 4 October 1834.

caption: The centre of the Milky Way in submillimetre and infrared light, imaged by the APEX telescope and 2MASS
story: This colour composite looks toward the heart of our Milky Way, about 26 000 light-years from Earth. It combines two very different kinds of light to show both the stars and the giant clouds of gas and dust around them.

The gas and dust clouds come from the LABOCA instrument on the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment, or APEX, which observes at submillimetre wavelengths, around 870 micrometres. Cold dust that is dark in ordinary light glows at these long wavelengths, so APEX can map clouds that would otherwise stay hidden.

The starlight comes from the 2MASS project, which surveyed the sky in three near-infrared bands. Near-infrared light slips through much of the dust that blocks our view of the galactic centre in visible light. Putting both together shows how the stars and the raw material between them are arranged. The image spans a region roughly 100 light-years wide.

caption: Part of Hickson Compact Group 7, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: One spiral galaxy dominates the foreground of this Hubble image, with many more distant galaxies scattered across the background. It belongs to Hickson Compact Group 7, or HCG 7, a tight grouping of three spiral galaxies and one lens-shaped, or lenticular, galaxy.

Crowded groups like this matter because their galaxies evolve differently from those in emptier parts of the Universe. A Hubble study charted three hundred young star clusters and 150 globular clusters in HCG 7, and found that star formation has been fairly steady over time, though high in the central regions.

Here is the puzzle. Other studies hint that the galaxies turned their gas into stars without any help from mergers. Yet they are using up their gas at a rate that suggests past mergers. Either the group has evolved calmly, or some process not yet understood is at work.
explore: The picture comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, and covers a field 3.3 by 3.0 arcminutes. The group lies about 200 million light-years away in the constellation Cetus.

story: This photo shows the central region of the spiral galaxy ESO 269-57, about 150 million light-years away in the southern constellation Centaurus. Its bright centre is overexposed here, and it is surrounded by a ring, a feature built into its classification.

Astronomers label it type Sar, with the "r" standing for that ring. Around the galaxy, many other galaxies at about the same distance form a loose cluster, and fainter, more distant galaxies sit in the background.

The name has its own story. It comes from the ESO/Uppsala Survey of the Southern Sky, carried out in the 1970s, which catalogued over 15,000 southern galaxies. The photo itself was made with KUEYEN, one of the telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, combining three exposures in blue, yellow-green and red light, of 600, 300 and 300 seconds.
explore: The image quality is 0.7 arcseconds and the field covers 90 by 90 arcseconds, with north up and east to the left.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 5023, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: We see the spiral galaxy NGC 5023 edge-on in this Hubble image. Its arms are hidden by the angle, but the slim profile of its disc stretches across the frame. It lies over 30 million light-years away.

NGC 5023 belongs to the M51 group, whose brightest member is the Whirlpool Galaxy. By comparison NGC 5023 keeps to itself, sitting fairly isolated from its neighbours. Yet it is popular with astronomers, because edge-on discs let them study what lies above and below a galaxy's central plane.

By sorting the stars there by type and by how far along they are in their lives, researchers learn how galaxies evolve. A study of six edge-on spirals, including this one, found a trend suggesting that heating of the disc helps explain the stars found away from the plane. In this image alone, Hubble's sharp view counts over 30 000 separate bright stars.
explore: Those 30 000 stars are only a small fraction of the several billion the galaxy holds; the rest are too faint to separate even with Hubble.
NGC 5023 is also one of 14 disc galaxies in the GHOSTS survey, the largest study so far of the stars living in the outer regions of disc galaxies.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 1689 with a dark matter map overlaid, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A purple overlay covers the galaxy cluster Abell 1689 in this Hubble image. The purple is not something a camera recorded directly; it is a map of where the cluster's dark matter is thought to be, added on top of the photograph. Around the edges, distorted galaxies are clearly visible.

Abell 1689 acts as a gravitational lens, its mass bending the light of galaxies far behind it. That mass is partly ordinary matter, the kind that makes up stars and gas, and partly dark matter, which cannot be seen but has gravity all the same.

The shapes of the distorted background galaxies are the key clues. How they are stretched depends on how matter is spread through the lens, on the geometry between the cluster and the distant galaxies, and on how dark energy has shaped the geometry of the Universe. By reading those distortions, astronomers can map the unseen mass.

story: Long, prominent dust lanes run along the edges of the spiral arms of NGC 2397 in this Hubble image, showing as dark patches and streaks against the glow of starlight. It is a classic spiral galaxy, lying nearly 60 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Volans.

In many ways NGC 2397 is typical of spirals. Its central portion is dominated by older, yellow and red stars, while star formation carries on in its outer, bluer spiral arms. Young stars tend to be hot and blue, so the colour of a region hints at the age of the stars within it.

Hubble's sharp resolution makes it possible to study individual stars in nearby galaxies. In this view from the Advanced Camera for Surveys, the brightest of the young, blue stars in the arms can be picked out one by one, rather than blurring together into a general glow.

caption: The lenticular galaxy IC 335, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The galaxy IC 335 is seen edge-on in this Hubble image, set in front of a backdrop of distant galaxies. It belongs to a group of four galaxies within the Fornax Galaxy Cluster, which lies 60 million light-years away, and it measures 45 000 light-years long.

Viewing it edge-on makes classification tricky, because features like spiral arms or a central bar show only from the front. Still, IC 335 can be classed as an S0, or lenticular, galaxy. These sit between spirals and ellipticals: they have a thin disc and a bulge like a spiral, but have used up most of their gas, so few new stars form and their stars are mostly ageing.

Lenticulars are easily confused with ellipticals. Both evolve quietly today, but ellipticals had violent pasts. Lenticulars may be fading spirals that never interacted, or the result of a single merger. Their true nature is still debated.
explore: S0 and elliptical galaxies, despite their different shapes, share some traits, including typical sizes and features in their spectra. Both are known as early-type galaxies because they are evolving passively rather than actively forming stars.

That makes NGC 247 one of the closest galaxies to our Milky Way. Nearness matters in astronomy, because the closer a galaxy is, the more detail telescopes can resolve, from clusters of stars to clouds of gas.

NGC 247 is a member of the Sculptor Group, a small gathering of galaxies held together by gravity. Galaxies rarely live completely alone; most belong to groups or larger clusters, and those neighbours can influence how they grow and change. A spiral galaxy like this one is a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust with arms around a brighter centre. The filters used for this picture include one that isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, which highlights regions where stars are forming.
