caption: The northern part of the galaxy cluster Abell 1758, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble's view here covers the northern portion of the galaxy cluster Abell 1758, known as A1758N, approximately 3.2 billion light-years from Earth. A galaxy cluster is a huge gathering of galaxies bound together by gravity, among the largest structures in the Universe.

Abell 1758 is itself part of a larger structure made of two clusters, sitting some 2.4 million light-years apart. And A1758N is split again into two sub-sections, called East and West, or A1758NE and A1758NW.

Both sub-sections show disturbances, and that is strong evidence that they formed from smaller clusters colliding and merging. Clusters are thought to grow this way, by absorbing smaller groups over long stretches of time. Catching them in the act, with the signs of recent mergers still visible, helps astronomers understand how the biggest structures in the Universe are assembled.

A lens-shaped, or lenticular, galaxy has a disc and a central bulge but little ongoing star formation. Seeing one encircled by a ring tilted almost perpendicular to it is unusual, and the high resolution of this image makes both parts easy to tell apart.

NGC 4650A belongs to the Centaurus chain of galaxies, lying in the southern constellation that shares its name, about 165 million light-years away according to the caption. NGC 4605 belongs to the Messier 81 group, known for unusual members, many formed in galaxy collisions. With its somewhat odd shape, NGC 4605 fits the family, though the origin of its quirks is not yet clear.

Astronomers use it as a testing ground. Its young stars help show how interactions affect the birth and life of stars, and how stellar nurseries gather into clusters. It is also a test for dark matter: the way dark matter seems to be spread through its halo does not quite match what models predict, though the evidence is still inconclusive.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 7793, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the spiral arms and small central bulge of NGC 7793, crossed by a mottled pattern of dark dust. Its spiral structure is not strongly defined, and occasional bursts of bright pink mark stellar nurseries where new stars are forming. It lies in the constellation Sculptor, some 13 million light-years away according to the caption.

The calm appearance hides a violent object. Astronomers have found a powerful microquasar in the galaxy: a black hole feeding on material from a companion star. Full-sized quasars sit at galaxy centres, so finding one in a galaxy's disc is unusual.

Microquasars are like scale models that let astronomers study quasars up close. Material falling toward the black hole forms a swirling disc, and some of it is flung outward at very high speed in two opposite jets. Here the jets are blowing an expanding bubble of hot gas some 1,000 light-years across.
explore: NGC 7793 ranks among the brightest members of the Sculptor Group, one of the nearest galaxy groups to our Local Group, which contains the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds.

caption: The elliptical galaxy NGC 4889, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The elliptical galaxy NGC 4889 sits in front of hundreds of background galaxies in this Hubble image, deep inside the Coma galaxy cluster. It lies about 300 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices.

An elliptical galaxy is a smooth, rounded collection of stars without the arms or flat disc of a spiral. From the outside, NGC 4889 looks calm, set against hundreds of galaxies that lie much farther away.

What it hides is far more dramatic. Well out of sight of human eyes, a gigantic supermassive black hole sits at the galaxy's centre. A supermassive black hole is an object so dense that not even light escapes it, and such objects are thought to lie at the hearts of most large galaxies. This one cannot be seen in the picture at all; its presence is known from its effects rather than from any light it gives off.

caption: The overlapping galaxies NGC 3314, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two galaxies overlap in this highly detailed Hubble image of NGC 3314. At first they look as if they are crashing into each other, but that is an illusion.

This is a trick of perspective. The two galaxies simply happen to line up from our point of view on Earth, one sitting in front of the other along our line of sight. They are not touching and are not interacting.

Chance alignments like this can be useful. When a galaxy sits directly in front of another, light from the one behind shines through the nearer one. That backlight can reveal dust in the foreground galaxy that would otherwise be hard to see, silhouetting it against the glow. So a pair that at first seems like a collision becomes a natural experiment, letting astronomers study the structure of one galaxy using the light of another. The pair lies about 150 million light-years away in the constellation Hydra.

caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy UGC 9128, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows UGC 9128, a dwarf irregular galaxy. Hubble clearly resolves its individual stars, and many much more distant galaxies appear in the background.

Most galaxies are either elliptical or spiral, but some fall into a catch-all group called irregulars, with no well-defined shape. UGC 9128 is also a dwarf, probably containing only about one hundred million stars, a small fraction of what a large spiral like the Milky Way holds.

Dwarfs matter because big galaxies are thought to be built up through mergers of smaller ones, which makes dwarfs a kind of building block. Astronomers have asked whether dwarfs share the structure of big galaxies, with older stars in a rounded halo and younger stars in a flat disc. Observations of UGC 9128 suggest that it does.
explore: UGC 9128 lies about 8 million light-years away in the constellation Boötes, the Herdsman. Though fairly close, it is so faint that nobody found it until the twentieth century.

story: Rich lanes of dust and gas near the centre of this face-on spiral galaxy stand out against glowing clusters of newborn stars and pink clouds of hydrogen that signal ongoing star formation. This is NGC 4911, deep in the Coma Cluster, which the caption places 320 million light-years away, in the northern sky in Coma Berenices. Thousands of other galaxies fill the background.

Spirals near the cluster's centre are being reshaped by their neighbours. Wispy arcs in the outer arms of NGC 4911 are being pulled and distorted by a companion, NGC 4911A, at upper right. The stripped material will eventually spread through the cluster core, feeding its stars and star clusters that drift between galaxies.

The Coma Cluster holds almost 1,000 galaxies, so interactions and collisions are frequent. When galaxies of similar mass merge, they form ellipticals, which is why ellipticals are more common near the crowded centre.
explore: This natural-colour image needed 28 hours of exposure, combining data from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 and Advanced Camera for Surveys. Hubble's sharp cameras and long exposures made the faint outer details visible.

story: This Hubble image shows IC 2006, an elliptical galaxy, a smooth, rounded collection of stars without the arms of a spiral. It lies in the constellation Eridanus.

Massive elliptical galaxies like this one are common in today's Universe. They were once furiously forming stars, but at some point that activity shut down, and how they stopped, a process astronomers call quenching, is an astrophysical mystery.

Observations with Hubble and ESO's Very Large Telescope have offered a clue. They found that three billion years after the Big Bang, galaxies of this type were still making stars in their outskirts but no longer in their interiors. That suggests the shutdown began in their cores and then spread outward. Those findings came from studying distant galaxies rather than this particular image, which serves as an example of the kind of galaxy involved.

story: The trailing arms of the spiral galaxy NGC 2276 fill this Hubble image, a delicate pattern of bright spiral arms and dark dust lanes. It lies in the constellation of Cepheus.
At first glance it looks like countless other spirals. Look more closely, though, and the galaxy turns out to be strangely lopsided, as if one side had been pushed or pulled out of balance.

Two forces have shaped it. One is gravitational interaction, the pull between galaxies, which can bend and stretch a spiral's arms. The other is intense star formation, which can light up one part of a galaxy more than another. Together they have given NGC 2276 its uneven look. The picture was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 using filters from the ultraviolet to the near-infrared, which help reveal where young stars are forming.

story: This optical image shows the distant galaxy ISOHDFS 27, as captured by the Hubble Space Telescope. It spans about 7 arcseconds on the sky, a tiny angle, but at its distance of roughly 6,000 million light-years that corresponds to about 130,000 light-years across.
ISOHDFS 27 is classed as a massive spiral galaxy. Its main plane is tilted about 50 degrees to our line of sight, so we see it partly from the side rather than straight on.

The picture accompanied work with ESO's Very Large Telescope, which used the ISAAC instrument to spread the galaxy's infrared light into a spectrum. That lets astronomers study light from glowing hydrogen gas, which is emitted at a red wavelength but stretched into the infrared by the galaxy's great distance.

story: A ragged collection of stars and gas clouds makes up the dwarf galaxy DDO 68 in this Hubble image. Astronomers call it a cosmic oddity.

At first glance it looks like a galaxy that formed only recently, right in our own cosmic neighbourhood. So the question is whether DDO 68 is really as young as it appears, or whether its youthful look is hiding an older past.

A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy, far less massive than the Milky Way, and dwarfs are thought to be some of the building blocks from which larger galaxies grow. That makes an unusual one like DDO 68 especially interesting to study. DDO 68 lies about 40 million light-years away in the constellation Leo. The image combines visible and near-infrared light with a filter that isolates glowing hydrogen gas, which traces regions where stars are forming.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1433, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view shows NGC 1433, a nearby spiral galaxy about 32 million light-years from Earth, according to the caption. It is a very active type of galaxy called a Seyfert galaxy, a class that makes up 10% of all galaxies, and it has a very bright, glowing centre.

Galaxy cores fascinate astronomers. Astronomers think most, if not all, galaxies have a supermassive black hole at their centre, ringed by a disc of material falling inward. In Seyfert galaxies, ultraviolet light is thought to come partly from that disc, so ultraviolet observations help show how gas behaves near the black hole.

NGC 1433 is part of the Legacy ExtraGalactic UV Survey, LEGUS, which studies 50 nearby galaxies. The ALMA telescope has found a surprising spiral structure in the gas close to its centre, plus a jet flowing from the black hole for just 150 light-years, the smallest such outflow seen beyond our galaxy.
explore: Ultraviolet light from galaxies mainly traces the most recently formed stars. LEGUS is also intended as groundwork for later studies with ALMA and the James Webb Space Telescope.

caption: The central regions of the Circinus galaxy, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory
story: This composite looks into the heart of the nearby Circinus galaxy, about 12 million light-years away according to the caption. A blue source near the lower right corner stands out: the supernova SN 1996cr, finally identified more than a decade after it exploded.

Its discovery was a piece of detective work. In 2001 it was singled out as a bright, variable object in a Chandra X-ray image, but its identity as a supernova was only confirmed years later. Clues from a spectrum taken with ESO's Very Large Telescope prompted the team to search through data from 18 different telescopes, on the ground and in space, nearly all of it already sitting in archives.
Among supernovae of the last 25 years, SN 1996cr is one of the closest to us. Old archive data, pieced together, let astronomers reconstruct the history of an explosion nobody noticed at the time.

caption: The starburst galaxy NGC 3077, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Light from many huge young star clusters blazes at the centre of NGC 3077 in this Hubble image, and dusty tendrils lace the whole galaxy. Look closely and vast numbers of individual stars appear across the frame, along with a few far more distant galaxies seen right through NGC 3077.

At first glance NGC 3077 resembles a typical, fairly peaceful elliptical galaxy. Hubble reveals otherwise: it is a hotbed of very energetic star formation. It lies about 13 million light-years away in Ursa Major, the Great Bear, forming a triplet with two brighter neighbours, the graceful spiral Messier 81 and the peculiar starburst galaxy Messier 82.

Interactions among the three galaxies have stoked star formation in the core of NGC 3077. Though overshadowed by its neighbours, it is very active too, and looks like a toned-down version of Messier 82.
explore: William Herschel first saw NGC 3077 in 1801 with his 47 cm telescope in England, as he was nearing the end of his sky surveys. Each filter in this image had an exposure of about 27 minutes, and the field of view spans about 3.3 arcminutes.

story: Ribbons of dust cross the bright disc of the spiral galaxy NGC 4565 in this detailed Hubble close-up. At lower right, the dust stands out even more sharply against the rich yellow light of the star-filled central regions. The galaxy's core lies just out of frame in that direction.

NGC 4565 is one of the most famous edge-on spirals, turned so that we look straight into its glowing disc. Viewed whole, it shows up as a thin sliver of light, which has earned it the nickname the Needle Galaxy.

This edgewise view is much like our own view from the Solar System toward the core of the Milky Way, where dust also blocks part of the disc's light. At only about 40 million light-years away, the galaxy is fairly close, and it is big: roughly one third larger than the Milky Way. That makes it useful for comparing with our home.
explore: The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and spans about 3.4 by 3.4 arcminutes. Josh Barrington entered a version of it in Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

caption: The galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+223, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
scaleExtra: Light from this cluster took over 5 billion years to reach us, according to the caption.
story: Here Hubble captures the huge galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+223. Its light spent over 5 billion years travelling to reach us. A galaxy cluster is a vast gathering of galaxies held together by gravity, along with large amounts of unseen dark matter.

The cluster's enormous mass bends the light of objects far behind it. This effect, known as gravitational lensing, both magnifies and distorts the background galaxies, stretching and brightening them as seen from Earth.

Lensing can also do something stranger. Because light from a distant object can take more than one path around the cluster, the same object can appear several times in the image. This cluster is producing multiple images of the same distant objects in exactly this way. For astronomers, such repeated images are valuable: they help map how the cluster's mass is spread out, and they turn the cluster into a natural magnifying glass for studying galaxies that would otherwise be too faint to see.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from the near-infrared end of visible light into the infrared. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.

caption: The central region of the spiral galaxy NGC 247, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The nucleus of the spiral galaxy NGC 247 shows as a bright, whitish patch in this Hubble image, surrounded by stars, gas and dust. Dust makes dark patches and threads silhouetted on the starry background, and the gas has gathered into bright knots called H II regions, scattered mostly through the arms and outer areas.

NGC 247 is a relatively small spiral in the southern constellation Cetus, the Whale, around 11 million light-years away. It belongs to the Sculptor Group, which also contains the better-known Sculptor Galaxy, NGC 253.

The galaxy has a mysterious feature not seen here but clear in wider views. The northern part of its disc has an apparent void spanning almost a third of its length. The stars there are older, fainter and redder, suggesting star formation stopped there around one billion years ago. Recent studies suggest a gravitational encounter with part of another galaxy may be the cause.
explore: H II regions are clouds of hydrogen gas that have been ionised, or energised, by the light of hot young stars, which makes them glow.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 611, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
scaleExtra: The cluster lies roughly 3.2 billion light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.
story: Hundreds of small galaxies scatter across this view, some in shades of orange and others white. Most are fuzzy ovals, though a few show clear spiral arms. Many thin, long orange arcs curve around the centre of the image, where a strong orange glow sits. This is the galaxy cluster Abell 611, in the constellation Lynx.
Hubble released this inky image in celebration of Halloween, and the web of galaxies does have a cobweb feel. But the cluster is also a serious scientific target.

Those curved arcs are examples of strong gravitational lensing. The cluster's mass bends light from galaxies far behind it, stretching them into arcs around its centre. Because the amount of bending depends on how much mass the cluster contains, including dark matter that gives off no light, lensed arcs like these make Abell 611 a popular place to investigate dark matter.

caption: The galaxies NGC 4424 and LEDA 213994, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows two galaxies plainly. The larger is NGC 4424, and just below it sits a smaller, flatter, bright galaxy called LEDA 213994. Their names tell a story of their own.

A few cosmic objects have charming nicknames, like the Sombrero Galaxy or the Horsehead Nebula, but most are known only by catalogue entries. NGC 4424 comes from the New General Catalogue of Nebulae and Clusters of Stars, compiled in 1888. It has 7840 entries, mostly larger, brighter objects that early stargazers could spot more easily.

LEDA 213994 comes from the far more modern Lyon-Meudon Extragalactic Database, created in 1983 at the Lyon Observatory and containing millions of objects. Many NGC objects keep their older names simply because they were catalogued first. As for the acronym, LEDA may appeal partly because Leda was a princess in Ancient Greek mythology.
explore: Because the NGC ranks among the biggest catalogues in astronomy, many of Hubble's Pictures of the Week feature NGC objects. NGC 4424 lies about 30 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy Messier 77, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A glowing bar crosses the centre of this spiral galaxy, ringed by glittering stars and dust. From each side of the ring a spiral arm winds outward, and faint dark red dust clouds swirl through the disc. Six long rays and two short ones radiate from the core. This is Messier 77, a barred spiral 45 million light-years away in Cetus, the Whale.

The rays are diffraction spikes, made by Webb's optics, not the galaxy. They appear because the core is extremely bright and compact. It is an active galactic nucleus, powered by a supermassive black hole eight million times the mass of the Sun, where gas crashes together in tight orbit and releases enormous radiation.

The ring, more than 6 000 light-years across, is a starburst ring, packed with intense star formation seen as dense orange bubbles. Webb's view also reveals the central bar, which does not appear in visible-light images.
explore: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument adds the glow of interstellar dust in dark red, forming a huge vortex of swirling filaments with cavities between them. Along the southern arm, NIRCam also traces light from complex molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.

caption: The Wolf-Lundmark-Melotte galaxy, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: ESO's OmegaCAM camera on the VLT Survey Telescope captured this image of a solitary galaxy called Wolf-Lundmark-Melotte, or WLM for short. It lies in the direction of the constellation Cetus.
WLM belongs to our Local Group, the family of dozens of galaxies that includes the Milky Way. But it keeps its distance, sitting alone on the group's fringe as one of its farthest-flung members.

It is also small, and so isolated that it may never have interacted with another galaxy in the Local Group, and perhaps not with any other galaxy in the whole history of the Universe. Encounters between galaxies can stir up their gas and reshape them, so a galaxy that may have spent its whole history undisturbed is a notable case, a small system that has perhaps always kept to itself.
explore: The image was made as part of the VST/OmegaCAM Local Group Survey, using filters from the ultraviolet through visible light, including one that isolates glowing hydrogen.

caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy DDO 190, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Older reddish stars fill the outskirts of this small galaxy, while younger bluish stars shine in its more crowded middle. Pockets of gas heated by stars appear here and there, the most obvious one glowing toward the bottom. Behind it, many distant spiral, elliptical and shapeless galaxies glow. This is DDO 190, a dwarf irregular galaxy, small and without clear structure.

Our Solar System sits in a big spiral with plenty of dwarf companions. DDO 190 has no such company. It lies around nine million light-years away, according to the caption, loosely part of the Messier 94 group, yet its closest dwarf neighbour, DDO 187, is thought to lie at least three million light-years off.
By comparison, the Magellanic Clouds orbit the Milky Way at around a fifth of that distance, and even the Andromeda Galaxy is closer to us than DDO 190 is to its nearest neighbour.

story: A bright nucleus sits at the centre of a disc so thin it looks like a straight line in this Hubble image of NGC 4452. A hazy halo of stars around the galaxy makes it seem to glow. We see it almost exactly edge-on from Earth, an unusual angle on its billions of stars.

NGC 4452 belongs to the Virgo Cluster, an enormous grouping of around 2000 galaxies approximately 60 million light-years away. Our own Local Group is thought to lie on the cluster's fringes, and far in the future it may be pulled slowly into Virgo by gravity. Many faint galaxies much farther away appear in the background.

story: This colourful image from ESO's Very Large Telescope shows NGC 1055, a large galaxy in the constellation of Cetus, the Sea Monster. It is thought to be up to 15 percent wider than our own Milky Way.

NGC 1055 is classed as a spiral galaxy, yet it seems to lack the sweeping arms that spirals are known for. That is simply a matter of angle. We see it edge-on, so its disc appears as a narrow band and the arms are hidden from view, much as the pattern on a plate disappears when you look at it from the side.

What the edge-on view does reveal is something odd. The galaxy's structure shows strange twists rather than lying perfectly flat. These twists probably came from an interaction with a large neighbouring galaxy. The picture was made with the FORS2 instrument, using several filters, one of which isolates the glow of hydrogen gas.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 5068, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Thousands upon thousands of tiny stars fill this close-up of a spiral galaxy, crowded most densely in a whitish bar at its core. Clumps and threads of dust form an almost skeletal framework that follows the twist of a spiral arm, and large glowing bubbles of red gas are tucked into the dust. This is NGC 5068, a barred spiral about 17 million light-years away in Virgo, with its bar in the upper left.

Stars and planets are born inside clouds of gas and dust that block visible light. Webb's MIRI and NIRCam instruments see in infrared, letting astronomers look straight through the dust of NGC 5068 and watch star formation as it happens.

This portrait is part of a campaign to build a treasure trove of star-formation observations in nearby galaxies. Star formation matters across astronomy, from the thin plasma between stars to the growth of whole galaxies.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy Messier 95, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the spiral galaxy Messier 95, which also goes by M95 and NGC 3351. It lies about 35 million light-years away in Leo, the Lion. It is a barred spiral: a bar of stars cuts through its centre, surrounded by an inner ring that is busy forming new stars. Our own Milky Way is a barred spiral too.

The galaxy was discovered by Pierre Méchain in 1781 and catalogued by Charles Messier just four days later. Messier was mainly a comet hunter, often frustrated by fuzzy objects that looked like comets but were not, so he listed them in his famous catalogue to spare other astronomers the same confusion.

Messier 95 has also hosted a supernova, SN 2012aw, in one of its spiral arms. Comparing images from before and after, astronomers identified the star that had vanished: a huge red supergiant up to 26 times the mass of the Sun.
explore: A supernova marks the explosive end of a massive star's life. Finding the progenitor star in older images helps astronomers link what kinds of stars produce which kinds of explosions.

caption: The galaxy Messier 85, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Messier 85 appears in delicate, hazy glory in this atmospheric Hubble image. It lies around 50 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices, Berenice's Hair, and was first discovered by Pierre Méchain, a colleague of Charles Messier, in 1781.

It is an intriguing galaxy. Its properties sit partway between a lenticular and an elliptical galaxy, and it seems to be interacting with two neighbours out of frame: the spiral NGC 4394 and the small elliptical MCG 3-32-38.

It holds some 400 billion stars, most very old. But its centre hosts relatively young stars only a few billion years old, believed to be the product of a late burst of star birth, probably sparked by a merger with another galaxy more than four billion years ago. And while almost every galaxy is thought to host a supermassive black hole, star motions leave it unclear whether this one does.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 supplied the infrared, visible and ultraviolet data blended in this image.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1566, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The tiny yet intensely bright nucleus of NGC 1566 glitters at the centre of this Hubble image, framed by swirling, symmetrical lavender arms. According to the caption, the galaxy is about 40 million light-years away, in Dorado, the Dolphinfish.

It is classed as an intermediate spiral: it lacks a clearly defined bar of stars at its centre, but is not quite an unbarred spiral either. Its tiny, brilliant core marks it as a Seyfert galaxy, a type whose centres are very active and luminous, sending out strong bursts of radiation and possibly hosting supermassive black holes that outweigh the Sun many millions of times over.
Among known Seyfert galaxies, it ranks second in brightness. It also outshines and dominates every other member of the Dorado Group, one of the richest galaxy groups in the southern hemisphere.

caption: The interacting galaxy IC 1727, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The galaxy IC 1727 looks twisted and lopsided in this Hubble image, and its bright nucleus has been dragged off-centre. The cause lies just out of frame: its near neighbour, NGC 672, with which it is interacting.

Gravity pulls galaxies together into groups and clusters, and sometimes brings pairs close enough to tug on each other. The results can be extreme. Interacting galaxies are often badly distorted, torn apart, or driven to collide and merge into a single mass of gas, dust and stars.

Such encounters often trigger starbursts, flurries of intense star formation, and new star clusters, likely because gravity churns and compacts the gas and dust. Astronomers found that both IC 1727 and NGC 672 had simultaneous bursts of star formation, roughly 20 to 30 million years ago, and again around 450 to 750 million years ago. The likeliest explanation is that the pair swing close to each other every so often, stirring up gas and dust each time they pass.
explore: IC 1727 lies about 23 million light-years away in the constellation Triangulum.

caption: The young star cluster NGC 602, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A star cluster sits inside a large, many-coloured nebula of gas and dust. Dark ridges and peaks surround it, lit on their inner sides, with thin, translucent clouds draped over them. All around, a huge number of distant galaxies shine through, along with a few large, bright foreground stars. This is NGC 602, a young cluster on the fringes of the Small Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy about 200 000 light-years away.

Its surroundings resemble conditions in the early Universe, with very few elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. Dark clouds of dense dust and plenty of ionised gas suggest that stars are still forming, so the cluster offers a chance to study star birth under conditions very different from those near the Sun.
Using Webb, a team including Peter Zeidler, Elena Sabbi and Antonella Nota found candidates for the first young brown dwarfs detected outside our Milky Way.
explore: Brown dwarfs are objects too small to sustain nuclear fusion in their cores like true stars, which makes young ones faint and hard to find at such distances.

caption: The stellar nursery IC 2944 and the Thackeray globules, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: Thick, dark clouds of dust stand in silhouette against the pale pink glow of gas in this view of IC 2944, a stellar nursery. The dark clumps are known as the Thackeray globules.
The picture was released to mark a milestone: 15 years of operations for ESO's Very Large Telescope. Nearby hot young stars are bombarding the globules with fierce ultraviolet radiation.

The globules are in trouble. The radiation is wearing them away and breaking them into fragments, much as lumps of butter would on a hot frying pan. Dense clouds like these can sometimes collapse to form new stars, but these ones are unlikely to get the chance. They will probably be destroyed first, worn down by the radiation of their hot young neighbours before any stars can form inside them.
explore: IC 2944 lies about 6500 light-years away in the constellation Centaurus. The image was made with the FORS1 instrument, using filters including ones that isolate the glow of oxygen and hydrogen.
